det_01.label: Origin: The Economist's 2018 graphic-detail piece
det_01.content: On 24 November 2018 The Economist published a Graphic Detail piece titled 'TV's golden age is real' (print headline: 'The end of channel surfing'). The piece argued that the contemporary belief in a 'golden age' of television was, against many cultural pundits' instinct, supported by hard data. To make that case the paper pulled raw text dumps from IMDb's public interfaces, joined them with OMDb (Open Movie Database) for region and air-date metadata, and produced a season-level dataset of 2,266 American TV-drama seasons spanning 1990 to 2018. Each row represents a single season (e.g. Breaking Bad season 5) carrying an IMDb-weighted average rating, a 'share' of votes received by that season relative to the show, the air date of the season's first episode, and a list of genres. The CSV used in this analysis is the actual artifact behind that scatter chart, published openly in The Economist's graphic-detail-data GitHub repository.

det_02.label: How IMDb ratings are computed
det_02.content: The 'av_rating' column is not a simple arithmetic mean. IMDb publishes a weighted vote average: each individual rating is reweighted by an undisclosed algorithm that down-weights suspected manipulation and up-weights long-standing, frequent voters. IMDb refuses to disclose the exact formula precisely so that vote brigades can't game it. This matters for any blog claim: when we say 'Breaking Bad season 5 scored 9.7' we are reporting IMDb's weighted average of that season's episode ratings, not a raw user mean. The 'share' column in the CSV gives each season's portion of the title's total votes, which is an indirect proxy for relative audience engagement across seasons. Because the algorithm is opaque and updates several times per day, exact reproductions to two decimal places will drift; the dataset is a 2018-vintage snapshot.

det_03.label: The 'Golden Age of Television' thesis
det_03.content: The cultural shorthand 'Golden Age of Television' usually refers to a renaissance of dramatic television that critics date to January 1999 — the premiere of HBO's The Sopranos. Across the 2000s, anti-hero-driven prestige dramas (The Wire, Mad Men, Breaking Bad) raised the formal ambition of the medium until production values began to rival cinema. By the mid-2010s the same trend had broadened into 'Peak TV', a phrase coined by FX chief John Landgraf in 2015 to describe a glut of scripted series. The number of scripted originals on US television grew from 210 in 2009 to 495 in 2018, the year The Economist's article appeared. The dataset under analysis covers exactly this 1990–2018 arc, which makes it ideal for testing whether perceived improvement is reflected in viewer ratings.

det_04.label: Why HBO matters for the curve
det_04.content: Any analysis that finds an upward drift in IMDb ratings from the early 2000s onward will land squarely on the HBO/cable/streaming pivot. The Sopranos (1999), The Wire (2002), Six Feet Under (2001), and later Game of Thrones (2011) and Breaking Bad (2008, AMC) bent the format of serialized drama. Even in 2018, Six Feet Under's series-finale episode 'Everyone's Waiting' regularly tops 'best TV episode' lists, and until 2025 Breaking Bad's 'Ozymandias' was the only TV episode on IMDb with a perfect 10.0. These are the data points the eye is drawn to in any season-level scatter — the cluster of 9.0+ ratings that appears after 2000 and grows denser through the 2010s.

det_05.label: Why a general reader should care
det_05.content: TV is now the cultural form most Americans consume the most of, by hours. Whether the medium is genuinely 'better' than it used to be is a debate that animates cultural critics, network executives, and dinner-table arguments. The Economist's chart matters because it offered a rare data-grounded answer at a moment when subjective opinion ruled the conversation. It is also a useful natural experiment for anyone who wants to ask whether ratings inflation, audience self-selection, or genuine quality improvement explains the curve — and the dataset has all three signals (vote shares, genre, time) needed to interrogate that.

det_06.label: Survivorship and selection caveats
det_06.content: Three biases must be acknowledged before reading any trend out of this dataset. First, survivorship: shows that aired and were forgotten still appear, but only seasons that exist on IMDb at all make it in — very obscure pre-1995 dramas may be undercounted. Second, audience self-selection: IMDb voters skew young, male, online, and engaged; their tastes are not 'the median viewer'. Third, vote concentration: more recent shows have many more votes than older ones, so the weighted-average machinery is doing more smoothing on a 2017 season than on a 1992 season. Any rising-trend claim should therefore be hedged: it is a rise in IMDb-voter consensus, which is correlated with — but not identical to — a rise in 'objective' television quality.

det_07.label: Suggested analyses for the Analyst
det_07.content: Given the dataset's columns, the following lines of analysis are most likely to produce a defensible 'golden age' narrative: (1) yearly mean and median season rating from 1990 to 2018, with a count of seasons each year as context; (2) the count of seasons rated 9.0+ per year, since that threshold isolates the prestige-tier; (3) a genre breakdown — Drama, Crime, Sci-Fi, Mystery, etc. — to see whether the rise is broad or driven by one bucket; (4) the top 20 highest-rated seasons in the entire dataset, because those are the recognisable show titles a reader will care about; and (5) for each top show, the within-show season-by-season trajectory. Watch out for: thin sample sizes in the early 1990s, and shows that span the boundary (e.g. Frasier began in 1993 but its strongest seasons aired later).

det_08.label: External benchmark: what others found in the same data
det_08.content: Independent re-analyses by the Stat Significant blog and others, working with the same IMDb backbone but extending past 2018, report a sustained rise in series acclaim that begins in the early 2000s on the heels of The Sopranos and continues through the 2010s — with a flattening or mild decline emerging only around 2022-2023, after our dataset ends. So whatever upward drift we find in 1990-2018 is consistent with a longer-running and externally-validated trend, not a quirk of one paper's methodology.
